newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu says Jewish settlers in Hebron forever.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says Jewish settlers in Hebron forever.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promised right-wing supporters on Thursday that Jewish settlers would never be forced to leave the West Bank town of Hebron.
"The Jewish community in Hebron will not be uprooted -- not now, not tomorrow, never," he said in a speech to members of the National Religious Party, a key partner in his coalition government.

Around 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns Israel's previous Labour-led government promised a year ago to hand over for Palestinian self-rule.

Under a landmark 1993 Israel-PLO interim deal, the future of Hebron settlers and 130,000 other Jews living in the West Bank and Gaza -- which Israel captured in the 1967 war -- will be determined in talks on a final peace agreement to be reached by 1999.

Netanyhau opposed the 1993 deal that launched Palestinian self-rule but has vowed to withdraw troops from parts of Hebron once Palestinians agree to modifications aimed at better safeguarding settlers in the town.
The two sides have failed in four weeks of intensive talks to agree on terms for the withdrawal.
Israel has accused Palestinian President Yasser Arafat of stalling to rally international pressure against Israel. Palestinians say Israel wants to renege on its commitments.
More than two million Palestinians live in the West Bank and Gaza where the PLO hopes to establish an independent state.
Jewish setters in Hebron prevented Palestinian journalists from entering their enclave on Thursday to cover a tour of the area by Hebron Mayor Mustafa Natsheh.
In Jerusalem, hundreds of followers of the late anti-Arab rabbi Meir Kahane gathered on Thursday to mark his death, calling on the government to scrap peace deals with the PLO.

"We here -- many or few, it doesn't matter -- are the only people who can save the state of Israel," Kahane's son Binyamin addressed the gathering alongside other former leaders of the banned Kach and Kahane Chai groups.

One speaker announced a new movement would follow in the footsteps of the two groups which Israel outlawed in 1994 after a right-wing militant shot dead 29 Palestinian worhippers at a mosque in Hebron.
American-born Meir Kahane, who founded Kach and went on to serve in Israel's parliament, advocated forcibly evicting Arabs from Israel, the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
He was shot dead by Egyptian born U.S. citizen El Sayyid Nosair in November 1990.
